text_content: # Content Security Policy Cheat Sheet
normalized_text: # Content Security Policy Cheat Sheet

text_content: ## Introduction
normalized_text: ## Introduction

text_content: This article brings forth a way to integrate the __defense in depth__ concept to the client-side of web applications. By injecting the Content-Security-Policy (CSP) headers from the server, the browser is aware and capable of protecting the user from dynamic calls that will load content into the page currently being visited.
normalized_text: This article brings forth a way to integrate the __defense in depth__ concept to the client-side of web applications. By injecting the Content-Security-Policy (CSP) headers from the server, the browser is aware and capable of protecting the user from dynamic calls that will load content into the page currently being visited.

text_content: ## Context
normalized_text: ## Context

text_content: The increase in XSS (Cross-Site Scripting), clickjacking, and cross-site leak vulnerabilities demands a more __defense in depth__ security approach.
normalized_text: The increase in XSS (Cross-Site Scripting), clickjacking, and cross-site leak vulnerabilities demands a more __defense in depth__ security approach.

text_content: ### Defense against XSS
normalized_text: ### Defense against XSS

text_content: CSP defends against XSS attacks in the following ways:
normalized_text: CSP defends against XSS attacks in the following ways:

text_content: #### 1. Restricting Inline Scripts
normalized_text: #### 1. Restricting Inline Scripts

text_content: By preventing the page from executing inline scripts, attacks like injecting
normalized_text: By preventing the page from executing inline scripts, attacks like injecting

text_content:
```html

```


text_content: will not work.

text_content: #### 2. Restricting Remote Scripts
normalized_text: #### 2. Restricting Remote Scripts

text_content: By preventing the page from loading scripts from arbitrary servers, attacks like injecting

text_content:
```html

```

text_content: #### 3. Restricting Unsafe JavaScript
normalized_text: #### 3. Restricting Unsafe JavaScript

text_content: By preventing the page from executing text-to-JavaScript functions like `eval`, the website will be safe from vulnerabilities like the this:

text_content: #### 4. Restricting Form submissions
normalized_text: #### 4. Restricting Form submissions

text_content: By restricting where HTML forms on your website can submit their data, injecting phishing forms won't work either.
normalized_text: By restricting where HTML forms on your website can submit their data, injecting phishing forms won't work either.

```html

```

text_content: #### 5. Restricting Objects
normalized_text: #### 5. Restricting Objects

text_content: And by restricting the HTML [object](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/object) tag, it also won't be possible for an attacker to inject malicious flash/Java/other legacy executables on the page.

text_content: ### Defense against framing attacks
normalized_text: ### Defense against framing attacks

text_content: Attacks like clickjacking and some variants of browser side-channel attacks (xs-leaks) require a malicious website to load the target website in a frame.
normalized_text: Attacks like clickjacking and some variants of browser side-channel attacks (xs-leaks) require a malicious website to load the target website in a frame.

text_content: Historically the `X-Frame-Options` header has been used for this, but it has been obsoleted by the `frame-ancestors` CSP directive.
normalized_text: Historically the `X-Frame-Options` header has been used for this, but it has been obsoleted by the `frame-ancestors` CSP directive.

text_content: ### Defense in Depth
normalized_text: ### Defense in Depth

text_content: A strong CSP provides an effective __second layer__ of protection against various types of vulnerabilities, especially XSS. Although CSP doesn't prevent web applications from *containing* vulnerabilities, it can make those vulnerabilities significantly more difficult for an attacker to exploit.
normalized_text: A strong CSP provides an effective __second layer__ of protection against various types of vulnerabilities, especially XSS. Although CSP doesn't prevent web applications from *containing* vulnerabilities, it can make those vulnerabilities significantly more difficult for an attacker to exploit.

text_content: Even on a fully static website, which does not accept any user input, a CSP can be used to enforce the use of [Subresource Integrity (SRI)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Subresource_Integrity). This can help prevent malicious code from being loaded on the website if one of the third-party sites hosting JavaScript files (such as analytics scripts) is compromised.
normalized_text: Even on a fully static website, which does not accept any user input, a CSP can be used to enforce the use of [Subresource Integrity (SRI)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Subresource_Integrity). This can help prevent malicious code from being loaded on the website if one of the third-party sites hosting JavaScript files (such as analytics scripts) is compromised.

text_content: With all that being said, CSP __should not__ be relied upon as the only defensive mechanism against XSS. You must still follow good development practices such as the ones described in [Cross-Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet](Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md), and then deploy CSP on top of that as a bonus security layer.
normalized_text: With all that being said, CSP __should not__ be relied upon as the only defensive mechanism against XSS. You must still follow good development practices such as the ones described in [Cross-Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet](Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md), and then deploy CSP on top of that as a bonus security layer.

text_content: ## Policy Delivery
normalized_text: ## Policy Delivery

text_content: You can deliver a Content Security Policy to your website in three ways.
normalized_text: You can deliver a Content Security Policy to your website in three ways.

text_content: ### 1. Content-Security-Policy Header
normalized_text: ### 1. Content-Security-Policy Header

text_content: Send a Content-Security-Policy HTTP response header from your web server.
normalized_text: Send a Content-Security-Policy HTTP response header from your web server.

text_content:
```text
Content-Security-Policy: ...
```
normalized_text:
```text
Content-Security-Policy: ...
```

text_content: Using a header is the preferred way and supports the full CSP feature set. Send it in all HTTP responses, not just the index page.
normalized_text: Using a header is the preferred way and supports the full CSP feature set. Send it in all HTTP responses, not just the index page.

text_content: This is a W3C Spec standard header. Supported by Firefox 23+, Chrome 25+ and Opera 19+
normalized_text: This is a W3C Spec standard header. Supported by Firefox 23+, Chrome 25+ and Opera 19+

text_content: ### 2. Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only Header
normalized_text: ### 2. Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only Header

text_content: Using the `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`, you can deliver a CSP that doesn't get enforced.
normalized_text: Using the `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`, you can deliver a CSP that doesn't get enforced.

text_content:
```text
Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: ...
```
normalized_text:
```text
Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: ...
```

text_content: Still, violation reports are printed to the console and delivered to a violation endpoint if the `report-to` and `report-uri` directives are used.
normalized_text: Still, violation reports are printed to the console and delivered to a violation endpoint if the `report-to` and `report-uri` directives are used.

text_content: This is also a W3C Spec standard header. Supported by Firefox 23+, Chrome 25+ and Opera 19+, whereby the policy is non-blocking ("fail open") and a report is sent to the URL designated by the `report-uri` (or newer `report-to`) directive. This is often used as a precursor to utilizing CSP in blocking mode ("fail closed")
normalized_text: This is also a W3C Spec standard header. Supported by Firefox 23+, Chrome 25+ and Opera 19+, whereby the policy is non-blocking ("fail open") and a report is sent to the URL designated by the `report-uri` (or newer `report-to`) directive. This is often used as a precursor to utilizing CSP in blocking mode ("fail closed")

text_content: Browsers fully support the ability of a site to use both `Content-Security-Policy` and `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` together, without any issues. This pattern can be used for example to run a strict `Report-Only` policy (to get many violation reports), while having a looser enforced policy (to avoid breaking legitimate site functionality).
normalized_text: Browsers fully support the ability of a site to use both `Content-Security-Policy` and `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` together, without any issues. This pattern can be used for example to run a strict `Report-Only` policy (to get many violation reports), while having a looser enforced policy (to avoid breaking legitimate site functionality).

text_content: ### 3. Content-Security-Policy Meta Tag
normalized_text: ### 3. Content-Security-Policy Meta Tag

text_content: Sometimes you cannot use the Content-Security-Policy header if you are, e.g., Deploying your HTML files in a CDN where the headers are out of your control.
normalized_text: Sometimes you cannot use the Content-Security-Policy header if you are, e.g., Deploying your HTML files in a CDN where the headers are out of your control.

text_content: In this case, you can still use CSP by specifying a `http-equiv` meta tag in the HTML markup, like so:
normalized_text: In this case, you can still use CSP by specifying a `http-equiv` meta tag in the HTML markup, like so:

text_content:
```html
<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="...">
```
normalized_text:
```html
<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="...">
```

text_content: Almost everything is still supported, including full XSS defenses. However, you will not be able to use [framing protections](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/frame-ancestors), [sandboxing](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/sandbox), or a [CSP violation logging endpoint](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/report-to).
normalized_text: Almost everything is still supported, including full XSS defenses. However, you will not be able to use [framing protections](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/frame-ancestors), [sandboxing](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/sandbox), or a [CSP violation logging endpoint](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/report-to).

text_content: ### WARNING
normalized_text: ### WARNING

text_content: __DO NOT__ use `X-Content-Security-Policy` or `X-WebKit-CSP`. Their implementations are obsolete (since Firefox 23, Chrome 25), limited, inconsistent, and incredibly buggy.
normalized_text: __DO NOT__ use `X-Content-Security-Policy` or `X-WebKit-CSP`. Their implementations are obsolete (since Firefox 23, Chrome 25), limited, inconsistent, and incredibly buggy.

text_content: ## CSP Types (granular/allowlist based or strict)
normalized_text: ## CSP Types (granular/allowlist based or strict)

text_content: For original research on allowlist weaknesses, see [CSP Is Dead, Long Live CSP!](https://research.google/pubs/csp-is-dead-long-live-csp-on-the-insecurity-of-whitelists-and-the-future-of-content-security-policy/).
normalized_text: For original research on allowlist weaknesses, see [CSP Is Dead, Long Live CSP!](https://research.google/pubs/csp-is-dead-long-live-csp-on-the-insecurity-of-whitelists-and-the-future-of-content-security-policy/).

text_content: The original mechanism for building a CSP involved creating allow-lists which would define the content and sources that were permitted in the context of the HTML page.
normalized_text: The original mechanism for building a CSP involved creating allow-lists which would define the content and sources that were permitted in the context of the HTML page.

text_content: However, current leading practice is to create a "Strict" CSP which is much easier to deploy and more secure as it is less likely to be bypassed.
normalized_text: However, current leading practice is to create a "Strict" CSP which is much easier to deploy and more secure as it is less likely to be bypassed.

text_content: ## Strict CSP
normalized_text: ## Strict CSP

text_content: A strict CSP can be created by using a limited number of the granular [Fetch Directives listed below](#fetch-directives) along with one of two mechanisms:
normalized_text: A strict CSP can be created by using a limited number of the granular [Fetch Directives listed below](#fetch-directives) along with one of two mechanisms:

text_content:
- Nonce based
- Hash based
normalized_text:
- Nonce based
- Hash based

text_content: The `strict-dynamic` directive can optionally also be used to make it easier to implement a Strict CSP.
normalized_text: The `strict-dynamic` directive can optionally also be used to make it easier to implement a Strict CSP.

text_content: The following sections will provide some basic guidance to these mechanisms but it is strongly recommended to follow Google's detailed and methodological instructions for creating a Strict CSP:
normalized_text: The following sections will provide some basic guidance to these mechanisms but it is strongly recommended to follow Google's detailed and methodological instructions for creating a Strict CSP:

text_content: __[Mitigate cross-site scripting (XSS) with a strict Content Security Policy (CSP)](https://web.dev/strict-csp/)__
normalized_text: __[Mitigate cross-site scripting (XSS) with a strict Content Security Policy (CSP)](https://web.dev/strict-csp/)__

text_content: ### Nonce based
normalized_text: ### Nonce based

text_content: Nonces are unique one-time-use random values that you generate for each HTTP response, and add to the Content-Security-Policy header, like so:
normalized_text: Nonces are unique one-time-use random values that you generate for each HTTP response, and add to the Content-Security-Policy header, like so:

text_content: You would then pass this nonce to your view (using nonces requires a non-static HTML) and render script tags that look something like this:
normalized_text: You would then pass this nonce to your view (using nonces requires a non-static HTML) and render script tags that look something like this:

text_content:
```html
<script nonce="<%= nonce %>">
    ...
</script>
```
normalized_text:
```html
<script nonce="<%= nonce %>">
    ...
</script>
```

text_content: #### Warning
normalized_text: #### Warning

text_content: __Don't__ create a middleware that replaces all script tags with "script nonce=..." because attacker-injected scripts will then get the nonces as well. You need an actual HTML templating engine to use nonces.
normalized_text: __Don't__ create a middleware that replaces all script tags with "script nonce=..." because attacker-injected scripts will then get the nonces as well. You need an actual HTML templating engine to use nonces.

text_content: ### Hashes
normalized_text: ### Hashes

text_content: When inline scripts are required, the `script-src 'hash_algo-hash'` is another option for allowing only specific scripts to execute.
normalized_text: When inline scripts are required, the `script-src 'hash_algo-hash'` is another option for allowing only specific scripts to execute.

text_content:
```text
Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'sha256-V2kaaafImTjn8RQTWZmF4IfGfQ7Qsqsw9GWaFjzFNPg='
```
normalized_text:
```text
Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'sha256-V2kaaafImTjn8RQTWZmF4IfGfQ7Qsqsw9GWaFjzFNPg='
```

text_content: To get the hash, look at Google Chrome developer tools for violations like this:
normalized_text: To get the hash, look at Google Chrome developer tools for violations like this:

text_content: > ❌ Refused to execute inline script because it violates the following Content Security Policy directive: "..." Either the 'unsafe-inline' keyword, a hash (__'sha256-V2kaaafImTjn8RQTWZmF4IfGfQ7Qsqsw9GWaFjzFNPg='__), or a nonce...
normalized_text: > ❌ Refused to execute inline script because it violates the following Content Security Policy directive: "..." Either the 'unsafe-inline' keyword, a hash (__'sha256-V2kaaafImTjn8RQTWZmF4IfGfQ7Qsqsw9GWaFjzFNPg='__), or a nonce...

text_content: You can also use this [hash generator](https://report-uri.com/home/hash). This is a great [example](https://csp.withgoogle.com/docs/faq.html#static-content) of using hashes.
normalized_text: You can also use this [hash generator](https://report-uri.com/home/hash). This is a great [example](https://csp.withgoogle.com/docs/faq.html#static-content) of using hashes.

text_content: #### Note
normalized_text: #### Note

text_content: Using hashes can be a risky approach. If you change *anything* inside the script tag (even whitespace) by, e.g., formatting your code, the hash will be different, and the script won't render.
normalized_text: Using hashes can be a risky approach. If you change *anything* inside the script tag (even whitespace) by, e.g., formatting your code, the hash will be different, and the script won't render.

text_content: ### strict-dynamic
normalized_text: ### strict-dynamic

text_content: The `strict-dynamic` directive can be used as part of a Strict CSP in combination with either hashes or nonces.
normalized_text: The `strict-dynamic` directive can be used as part of a Strict CSP in combination with either hashes or nonces.

text_content: If a script block which has either the correct hash or nonce is creating additional DOM elements and executing JS inside of them, `strict-dynamic` tells the browser to trust those elements as well without having to explicitly add nonces or hashes for each one.
normalized_text: If a script block which has either the correct hash or nonce is creating additional DOM elements and executing JS inside of them, `strict-dynamic` tells the browser to trust those elements as well without having to explicitly add nonces or hashes for each one.

text_content: Note that while `strict-dynamic` is a CSP level 3 feature, CSP level 3 is very widely supported in common, modern browsers.
normalized_text: Note that while `strict-dynamic` is a CSP level 3 feature, CSP level 3 is very widely supported in common, modern browsers.

text_content: For more details, check out [strict-dynamic usage](https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-csp/#strict-dynamic-usage).
normalized_text: For more details, check out [strict-dynamic usage](https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-csp/#strict-dynamic-usage).

text_content: ## Detailed CSP Directives
normalized_text: ## Detailed CSP Directives

text_content: Multiple types of directives exist that allow the developer to control the flow of the policies granularly. Note that creating a non-Strict policy that is too granular or permissive is likely to lead to bypasses and a loss of protection.
normalized_text: Multiple types of directives exist that allow the developer to control the flow of the policies granularly. Note that creating a non-Strict policy that is too granular or permissive is likely to lead to bypasses and a loss of protection.

text_content: ### Fetch Directives
normalized_text: ### Fetch Directives

text_content: Fetch directives tell the browser the locations to trust and load resources from.
normalized_text: Fetch directives tell the browser the locations to trust and load resources from.

text_content: Most fetch directives have a certain [fallback list specified in w3](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/#directive-fallback-list). This list allows for granular control of the source of scripts, images, files, etc.
normalized_text: Most fetch directives have a certain [fallback list specified in w3](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/#directive-fallback-list). This list allows for granular control of the source of scripts, images, files, etc.

text_content:
- `child-src` allows the developer to control nested browsing contexts and worker execution contexts.
- `connect-src` provides control over fetch requests, XHR, eventsource, beacon and websockets connections.
- `font-src` specifies which URLs to load fonts from.
- `img-src` specifies the URLs that images can be loaded from.
- `manifest-src` specifies the URLs that application manifests may be loaded from.
- `media-src` specifies the URLs from which video, audio and text track resources can be loaded from.
- `prefetch-src` was an experimental directive for prefetch/prerender resource URLs. It was __removed from the CSP Level 3 specification__ and is ignored by modern browsers — do not rely on it for defense. Constrain scripts, styles, and default fetches with the standard fetch directives instead.
- `object-src` specifies the URLs from which plugins can be loaded from.
- `script-src` specifies the locations from which a script can be executed from. It is a fallback directive for other script-like directives.
    - `script-src-elem` controls the location from which execution of script requests and blocks can occur.
    - `script-src-attr` controls the execution of event handlers.
- `style-src` controls from where styles get applied to a document. This includes `<link>` elements, `@import` rules, and requests originating from a `Link` HTTP response header field.
    - `style-src-elem` controls styles except for inline attributes.
    - `style-src-attr` controls styles attributes.
- `default-src` is a fallback directive for the other fetch directives. Directives that are specified have no inheritance, yet directives that are not specified will fall back to the value of `default-src`.

text_content: ### Document Directives
normalized_text: ### Document Directives

text_content: Document directives instruct the browser about the properties of the document to which the policies will apply to.
normalized_text: Document directives instruct the browser about the properties of the document to which the policies will apply to.

text_content:
- `base-uri` specifies the possible URLs that the `<base>` element can use.
- `plugin-types` has been [removed from the CSP specification](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=220724). Do not rely on it to enforce content types. Use `object-src 'none'` when embedded objects are unnecessary, as in the [strict policy examples](#strict-policy).
- `sandbox` restricts a page's actions such as submitting forms.
    - Only applies when used with the request header `Content-Security-Policy`.
    - Not specifying a value for the directive activates all of the sandbox restrictions. `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox;`
    - [Sandbox syntax](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/sandbox#Syntax)

text_content: ### Navigation Directives
normalized_text: ### Navigation Directives

text_content: Navigation directives instruct the browser about the locations that the document can navigate to or be embedded from.
normalized_text: Navigation directives instruct the browser about the locations that the document can navigate to or be embedded from.

text_content:
- `form-action` restricts the URLs which the forms can submit to.
- `frame-ancestors` restricts the URLs that can embed the requested resource inside of  `<frame>`, `<iframe>`, `<object>`, `<embed>`, or `<applet>` elements.
    - If this directive is specified in a `<meta>` tag, the directive is ignored.
    - This directive doesn't fallback to the `default-src` directive.
    - `X-Frame-Options` is rendered obsolete by this directive and is ignored by the user agents.

    - This directive doesn't fallback to the `default-src` directive.
    - `X-Frame-Options` is rendered obsolete by this directive and is ignored by the user agents.

text_content: ### Reporting Directives
normalized_text: ### Reporting Directives

text_content: Reporting directives deliver violations of prevented behaviors to specified locations. These directives serve no purpose on their own and are dependent on other directives.
normalized_text: Reporting directives deliver violations of prevented behaviors to specified locations. These directives serve no purpose on their own and are dependent on other directives.

text_content:
- `report-to` (CSP Level 3, used together with the [Reporting API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Reporting_API)) is the __primary, current__ reporting directive. It references an endpoint name defined in the [Reporting-Endpoints response header](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Reporting-Endpoints#syntax), which uses comma-separated `name="URL"` entries. The legacy `Report-To` header uses JSON instead.
    - [MDN report-to documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/report-to)
- `report-uri` is __deprecated__ by CSP Level 3 in favor of `report-to`. It takes a URI that reports are sent to.
    - Format: `Content-Security-Policy: report-uri https://example.com/csp-reports`
normalized_text:
- `report-to` (CSP Level 3, used together with the [Reporting API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Reporting_API)) is the __primary, current__ reporting directive. It references an endpoint name defined in the [Reporting-Endpoints response header](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Reporting-Endpoints#syntax), which uses comma-separated `name="URL"` entries. The legacy `Report-To` header uses JSON instead.
    - [MDN report-to documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/report-to)
- `report-uri` is __deprecated__ by CSP Level 3 in favor of `report-to`. It takes a URI that reports are sent to.
    - Format: `Content-Security-Policy: report-uri https://example.com/csp-reports`

text_content: For backward compatibility, declare both directives in conjunction. Browsers that support `report-to` will use it and ignore `report-uri`; older browsers fall back to `report-uri`. Once support for legacy browsers is no longer required, `report-uri` can be removed.

text_content: A strict policy's role is to protect against classical stored, reflected, and some of the DOM XSS attacks and should be the optimal goal of any team trying to implement CSP.

text_content: ### Basic non-Strict CSP Policy
normalized_text: ### Basic non-Strict CSP Policy

text_content: This policy can be used if it is not possible to create a Strict Policy and it prevents cross-site framing and cross-site form-submissions. It will only allow resources from the originating domain for all the default level directives and will not allow inline scripts/styles to execute.
normalized_text: This policy can be used if it is not possible to create a Strict Policy and it prevents cross-site framing and cross-site form-submissions. It will only allow resources from the originating domain for all the default level directives and will not allow inline scripts/styles to execute.

text_content: If your application functions with these restrictions, it drastically reduces your attack surface and works with most modern browsers.
normalized_text: If your application functions with these restrictions, it drastically reduces your attack surface and works with most modern browsers.

text_content: The most basic policy assumes:
normalized_text: The most basic policy assumes:

text_content:
- All resources are hosted by the same domain of the document.
- There are no inlines or evals for scripts and style resources.
- There is no need for other websites to frame the website.
- There are no form-submissions to external websites.

- There are no inlines or evals for scripts and style resources.

text_content: ### Preventing framing attacks (clickjacking, cross-site leaks)
normalized_text: ### Preventing framing attacks (clickjacking, cross-site leaks)

text_content:
- To prevent all framing of your content use:
    - `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none';`
- To allow for the site itself, use:
    - `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';`
- To allow for trusted domain, do the following:
    - `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors trusted.com;`
normalized_text:
- To prevent all framing of your content use:
    - `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none';`
- To allow for the site itself, use:
    - `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';`
- To allow for trusted domain, do the following:
    - `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors trusted.com;`

text_content: ### Refactoring inline code

text_content: When `default-src` or `script-src*` directives are active, CSP by default disables any JavaScript code placed inline in the HTML source, such as this:

```javascript
<script>
```

text_content: The inline code can be moved to a separate JavaScript file and the code in the page becomes:

```javascript
</script>
```
